readings.title: Who Owns a Museum?
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
On a rainy Tuesday, the North Quay Museum opened a small exhibition about the town's former textile mills. The objects were modest: a lunch tin, a time card, a patched apron and a photograph of workers outside a gate. Yet the room was unusually busy. Several visitors had worked in the mills, and they had come to hear what the museum would say about their lives.

The curator, Eva, had first written labels based on company records. They listed dates, machines and production figures. During a trial opening, however, one visitor pointed to the apron and explained why its pockets were uneven: workers had sewn extra space for tools they were expected to carry. Another remembered that the official photograph had been taken on a holiday, when the factory was closed. The records were accurate, but they did not tell the whole story.

Eva invited former workers to add short recorded comments. She also kept the original labels so that visitors could compare sources. Some memories disagreed. Rather than choosing one as the final truth, the museum displayed both accounts with the speakers' names and dates. A note explained that people remember events from different positions, and that a useful historical account may show where evidence is uncertain.

This approach created practical difficulties. Recordings required permission, translation for visitors who spoke other languages, and quiet headphones so that the voices would not fill the gallery. Staff also had to resist the temptation to treat every personal story as proof of a general pattern. They checked claims against pay books and local newspapers when possible.

By the end of the month, the museum had received new donations, but Eva valued something less visible: more residents now saw the building as a place where they could ask questions. The exhibition did not hand ownership of the collection to any single group. It made the work of interpreting it more open, while preserving the museum's duty to explain how it knew what it claimed.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：信息、推断与主旨

readings.title: The Second Life of a School Lunch
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
At Brookfield School, the bins after lunch used to contain almost as much food as the tables. Students blamed large servings; kitchen staff thought the menu was the problem. Instead of guessing, a student council measured what was thrown away for two weeks. They sorted unopened items from partly eaten meals and recorded the results without naming individual pupils. The surprising finding was that most waste came from side dishes chosen in a hurry.

The school tried a small change. Pupils could take a half serving of a side dish and return for more after eating it. The kitchen continued to prepare enough food, but served it in smaller batches. This meant that late arrivals still had a choice. The council put simple signs beside the dishes, describing ingredients rather than telling anyone to clean a plate.

After a month, the amount of food in the bins had fallen. The council was pleased, but its report included a caution. A quiet week of exams may have changed attendance, and fewer pupils may simply have chosen the hot lunch. To understand the change, the council compared waste with the number of meals served. Even then, it could say only that the new system was associated with less waste, not that it was the sole cause.

There was also a question of fairness. Some students worried that taking a small portion might be seen as refusing the cook's effort. Kitchen staff explained that asking for more was welcome and that different appetites were normal. The school made sure no one had to announce a reason for choosing a smaller plate.

The project did not end at the bin. The class studied the energy and water used before food reaches a dining room. They learned that throwing away a vegetable also wastes the work of growing, transporting and preparing it. At the final assembly, the council recommended continuing the flexible servings and measuring waste again next term. Their strongest message was simple: good intentions become more useful when people check what happens in practice.

readings.title: The River Notebook
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Every Thursday evening, residents of Elmbank walked to the footbridge with small notebooks. Their task was to record the river's colour, the amount of floating litter and the water level shown on a marked post. The project had been started by a science teacher, but anyone could join.

At first, volunteers wrote descriptions such as “rather high” or “quite muddy.” These phrases were understandable to neighbours, yet difficult to compare across weeks. The group therefore agreed on a short guide: five water-level marks, three colour categories and a count of visible litter items within a fixed stretch. They also recorded the time and recent rain. The new rules did not make the observers perfect, but they made the notes more consistent.

One autumn, several notebooks showed that the river became cloudy after rain even when the litter count stayed low. A few people immediately blamed a construction site upstream. The teacher reminded them that the notebooks could show a pattern, not its cause. Soil washed from gardens or paths might also explain the cloudiness. The group shared its records with a local environmental office, which could collect samples and investigate further.

The office later found several possible sources of loose soil and asked landowners to improve drainage. It did not announce a single culprit. Volunteers were disappointed by the lack of a dramatic answer, but they began to value a different result: their regular observations had helped officials decide where to look. They also noticed that a sudden change was easier to identify because ordinary days had been recorded too.

At the project's second anniversary, the teacher handed the notebooks to a new volunteer coordinator. She said the river belonged to no one observer, and neither did the data. Keeping a common method and sharing uncertainty made their simple records useful beyond the footbridge. The work showed how citizens can contribute to science without pretending that one set of observations answers every question.

readings.title: A Classroom After Twenty Years
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
When Mei enrolled in an evening accounting course, she had not sat in a classroom for twenty years. She had spent most of that time managing a repair shop, ordering supplies and speaking with customers. On the first night she worried that younger classmates would understand the software immediately while she searched for the right keys. She nearly turned around at the classroom door.

The instructor began by asking everyone to describe a problem they had solved outside school. Mei spoke about tracing a missing order through several handwritten records. A younger student described organising a music event. The instructor used both stories to introduce the idea of checking information before making a decision. Mei realised that she already used part of the course's logic, although she did not yet know its technical terms.

Learning the software was still difficult. At home, Mei could complete an exercise only by following a list of steps. When an unexpected message appeared on the screen, she froze. The instructor suggested that she write down what she expected, what actually happened and one possible cause. This short record helped her ask precise questions in class. It also showed her that mistakes could be examined instead of hidden.

Mei's classmates helped in different ways. One showed her a keyboard shortcut; she explained how real customers sometimes described a problem inaccurately. Their exchanges worked because neither kind of experience was treated as a complete answer. Once, Mei gave advice too quickly and discovered that a classmate needed time to test an idea alone. After that, she asked before offering help.

At the end of the term, Mei passed the course and used a spreadsheet at the shop. She did not become the fastest user of the program. What changed most was her willingness to approach a new task: she could connect it to what she knew, identify what she did not know and seek help without feeling that her earlier years had been wasted. Returning to study had added a new method to an existing life.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese.

A public place becomes more welcoming when people can participate in different ways. At a museum, one visitor may read every label while another listens to a short recording. Neither approach is more valuable simply because it takes longer. What matters is whether the information is clear enough for visitors to make their own connections. Staff can ask people what helped them understand an exhibition and what remained confusing. They should also explain how an object or story was selected, especially when evidence is incomplete. Such openness does not remove disagreement, but it gives everyone a better basis for discussion. When visitors see that their questions are taken seriously, they are more likely to return and share what they have learned.
translation.explanation: 仅供自评。注意neither、what matters is whether及especially when所体现的比较、主语从句和条件语义；根据意义完整、语言准确和表达自然评分。
translation.referenceAnswer: 当人们能够以不同方式参与时，公共场所就会变得更加友好。在博物馆里，一位参观者可能阅读每一条说明文字，另一位则听一段简短录音。某种方式并不会仅仅因为花费时间更长就更有价值。重要的是，信息是否足够清楚，能让参观者建立自己的联系。工作人员可以询问人们，哪些内容帮助他们理解展览，哪些地方仍令人困惑。他们还应解释某件展品或某个故事是如何被选中的，尤其是在证据不完整时。这种开放态度不会消除分歧，却能为每个人的讨论提供更好的基础。当参观者发现自己的问题受到认真对待时，他们就更可能再次到访，并分享所学。

criteria.name: 意义完整
criteria.description: 准确传达不同参与方式、信息清晰度、证据和讨论等主要信息及逻辑关系。

criteria.name: 语言准确
criteria.description: 正确处理比较、从句、指代与关键动词，无严重误译。

criteria.name: 表达自然
criteria.description: 中文通顺，句间衔接清楚，符合汉语表达习惯。

writing.stem:
Write at least 100 words in English on the following topic: A Practical Way to Reduce Food Waste.

Your neighbourhood centre plans to invite residents to suggest one realistic action for reducing food waste at home or in shared spaces. Write a short proposal. Describe the action, explain how people would carry it out, identify one possible difficulty and suggest how to handle it. Explain why your idea would help the community. You may use an imagined example. Do not write your real name or contact details.
knowledgePoints: 写作：建议、问题与解决办法
writing.explanation: 仅供自评。范文提出共享临期食品的具体规则、潜在困难、应对办法及社区收益。其他合理方案也可得分，按任务完成、组织连贯、语言运用评分。
writing.sampleAnswer:
I suggest creating a weekly “use it soon” shelf at our neighbourhood centre. Residents could place unopened, clearly labelled food there if it is still safe to eat but they will not use it in time. A volunteer would check dates and storage instructions before accepting each item. Food that needs refrigeration would go into a supervised fridge instead of the shelf.

One difficulty is that people may be unsure whether an item is suitable. We could post simple rules and ask donors to speak to a volunteer when they have doubts. The centre should never accept food with damaged packaging or unclear dates.

The shelf would give useful food another chance before it is thrown away. It could also help neighbours talk about shopping habits and learn to plan meals more carefully. We should count the items shared each month so that we can improve the system based on what actually happens.

criteria.name: 任务完成
criteria.description: 提出可行行动，说明执行方法、一个困难、解决办法和社区收益。

criteria.name: 组织连贯
criteria.description: 结构清晰，段落和衔接适合简短建议文。

criteria.name: 语言运用
criteria.description: 词汇与语法基本准确，表达明确，达到规定词数。
